title: Aqueous Solutions, Acids and pH
seo_title: Year 11 Chemistry: Aqueous Solutions and Acidity Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_code: Chemistry Unit 2: Aqueous solutions and acidity
standard_text: Water as a solvent; concentration in mol/L, g/L and ppm; solubility rules, precipitation reactions and ionic equations; acids and bases (Brønsted–Lowry), strong and weak acids, pH; neutralisation reactions and titrations. (Senior Secondary Chemistry, Unit 2: Molecular interactions and reactions)
meta_desc: Free Year 11 Chemistry worksheets on solutions and acids: concentration, dilution, ppm, precipitation, ionic equations, strong and weak acids, pH, neutralisation and titration calculations. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Each pH unit is a factor of 10 in [H⁺].
body_html:
How to think about it

Water is polar, so it dissolves many ionic and polar substances. Concentration c = n ÷ V (mol/L); for dilution c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. Mixing solutions can form an insoluble precipitate; the ionic equation leaves out spectator ions.

An acid donates protons (H⁺) and a base accepts them. Strong acids ionise fully; weak acids only partly. pH = −log[H⁺]. In a titration, the mole ratio in the equation links the acid and the base.

Example

pH of 0.0010 mol/L HCl?

[H⁺] = 0.0010

pH = −log 0.0010

Answer: 3

Example

25.0 mL of 0.100 mol/L NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 mL of HCl. c(HCl)?

n(NaOH) = 0.00250 mol

1 : 1, so 0.00250 ÷ 0.0200

Answer: 0.125 mol/L

Common mistakes

  • Mixing up strong and concentrated.
  • Forgetting to change mL into L in c = n ÷ V.
  • Ignoring the 2 : 1 ratio for H₂SO₄ in titrations.
